## SECTION 1 — MAIN STORY & CHRONOLOGICAL PLOT

### Pre-Outbreak Sequence

1. Jim Mercer drives through a severe storm on **Highway 13** toward Ravenwood late at night (approximately midnight)
2. Jim speaks with his wife **Sarah** by phone while driving — she urges him to stop for the night
3. Jim sees **something near the roadside trees** during a lightning flash — he never notices it consciously
4. Jim pulls into the **Ravenwood Hotel** parking lot
5. A **police cruiser** has someone pulled over near the hotel entrance — the stopped driver's head hangs unnaturally low and twitches
6. Jim optionally explores the parking lot before entering
7. Sarah calls again — Jim confirms he's stopping for the night
8. Jim enters the hotel lobby and checks in with **Earl Whitaker**
9. Jim meets lobby guests: **Cindy Sweets**, **Maria & Richard Dalton**, **Janeth Caldwell**
10. A **distant THUD** from upstairs disturbs the lobby briefly — Earl dismisses it as pipes
11. Jim freely explores the hotel pre-outbreak: lobby, bar, recreation room, west hallway, glimpses **Gerta** the maid
12. Jim encounters **Cindy Sweets** in the second-floor hallway outside Room 106 before entering his room
13. Jim enters **Room 104**, explores the room, attempts to text Sarah (fails — no signal)
14. Jim attempts to sleep — hears a **distant muffled scream** from somewhere inside the hotel
15. Jim reluctantly lies back down — fade to black

### Outbreak Sequence

16. Jim is jolted awake by a **civil emergency siren** and red emergency lights
17. Screaming, glass shattering, running footsteps erupt throughout the hotel
18. A **quarantine loudspeaker** broadcasts outside — cuts to static
19. **Gunshots** echo outside
20. Violent pounding and a man screaming erupt somewhere down the hallway
21. Jim exits Room 104 into the chaotic second-floor hallway
22. Jim encounters **Janeth Caldwell** crouching terrified in the upstairs hallway
23. Jim descends the stairwell toward the lobby
24. Jim discovers **Earl Whitaker** actively attacking a hotel guest near the reception desk — **first infected reveal**
25. Jim grabs a **baseball bat** from beneath overturned furniture
26. Jim fights Earl in the ruined lobby
27. **Janeth Caldwell** runs from upstairs toward the front entrance
28. A **police cruiser crashes through the hotel front doors** — Janeth is pinned and killed against a lobby pillar
29. The **Deadlock Protocol** is announced over the police radio
30. Jim searches Earl's body — obtains the **Manager's Key**
31. Jim enters the staff hallway and discovers the **Manager's Office** — first safe room established
32. Jim discovers the **VERN terminal**, **security monitors**, **guest ledger**, and **incident report**
33. Jim examines the **breaker panel** — East Wing and West Wing switches identified
34. Jim reads the **emergency lockdown notice** — courtyard identified as escape route
35. Jim activates **East Wing power** — electronic security doors in East Wing disengage
36. Jim navigates the East Wing hallway, discovers the **maintenance closet**, obtains the **screwdriver**
37. Jim navigates the **service stairwell** to the West Wing maintenance area
38. Jim locates the **West Wing maintenance office** via a maintenance access panel
39. Jim removes the **auxiliary fuse** — nearby lights shut down
40. Jim returns to the Manager's Office and installs the fuse — **West Wing power restored**
41. Courtyard security systems come online
42. Jim returns through the upper hallway — **Cindy Sweets jumpscare** at Room 106 — Cindy is dragged back into the room violently
43. Jim progresses through the West Wing — discovers the **Red Room**
44. Jim encounters the **infected lounge singer** — Red Room combat encounter
45. Jim navigates the backstage hallway to the **Courtyard Security Office**
46. Jim activates **courtyard access** remotely
47. Jim returns through the lobby — **infected police officer jumpscare** from crashed cruiser
48. Jim defeats the officer — obtains the **handgun** (first firearm)
49. Jim exits into the **hotel courtyard**
50. Jim discovers the **north courtyard gate** is locked due to generator failure
51. Jim locates and restores the **courtyard backup generator**
52. The **maintenance shed erupts** — the **Caretaker** boss encounter begins
53. Jim defeats the Caretaker
54. Jim unlocks the **north courtyard gate** — exits into the dark streets of Ravenwood
55. Jim stares out at the city: *"What the hell happened here?"*

## SECTION 6 — LORE & BACKSTORY

### What Is Explicitly Established:

- Ravenwood is a small mountain town
- The Ravenwood Hotel has operated since 1956
- Earl Whitaker has worked the hotel for 32 years
- The storm is severe enough to flood county roads and force state police to turn traffic around
- The town "gets strange when the weather turns" — per Earl (dismissed by him as "old mountain town stories")
- A civil emergency siren activates during the outbreak — suggesting some form of pre-existing emergency alert infrastructure exists for Ravenwood
- An emergency quarantine / Deadlock Protocol is declared — suggesting governmental or military awareness of a potential outbreak scenario
- The infection causes: pale/wrong eyes, animalistic behavior, blood around the mouth, jaw dislocation, stiff movement, violent feeding on living humans
- Advanced infection stages produce **physical mutation** (demonstrated by the Caretaker) — bloated musculature, enlarged limbs, glowing eye tissue, exposed sinew
- Maria Dalton's incident report notes she was transported to **St. Dymphna Hospital** at 11:42 PM — the outbreak begins after this time

### What Is NOT Established (Flagged):

- **⚠️** The origin or cause of the infection is not explained

- **⚠️** What "something near the tree line" during the drive represents — never explained
- **⚠️** What "something near the cruiser" seen from Room 104 window represents
- **⚠️** Whether the town was already infected before the storm or whether the storm is connected to the outbreak
- **⚠️** Who or what declared Deadlock Protocol and what their full plan is

> The manuscript contains a **structural duplication issue** between **Tab 08** and **Tab 09:**

> - **Tab 09 (Scene S6 & S7)** describes the player finding an *identical maintenance closet* with identical contents — including another screwdriver, identical maintenance note text, and identical Jim reaction line (*"…Fantastic."*)
>
> It appears the screwdriver and maintenance note discovery scene was written twice across two separate tabs, describing what should be the same event.
>

DEADLOCK PROTOCOL — GENERAL STORY OVERVIEW

Deadlock Protocol follows Jim Mercer, a field infrastructure engineer traveling through Appalachia during a severe storm.

Flooding, poor visibility, and worsening road conditions force Jim off Highway 13 and into the isolated town of Ravenwood. He stops at the Ravenwood Hotel for what he believes will be a single overnight stay.

The story begins slowly and grounded. Jim speaks with his wife Sarah by phone, explores the hotel, meets several guests and employees, and notices small signs that something is wrong around town.

The situation rapidly deteriorates.

An outbreak connected to Vanguard BioSystems and Project Ashen has begun spreading through Ravenwood. People begin mutating into violent creatures, public order collapses, and authorities initiate DEADLOCK PROTOCOL, effectively quarantining the town.

Jim is not a soldier sent to investigate the outbreak. He is an ordinary traveler trapped in Ravenwood who is trying to survive, understand what is happening, and ultimately get back to Sarah.

==================================================

RAVENWOOD HOTEL

==================================================

The Ravenwood Hotel is the opening major location and acts as the player's introduction to the survival-horror gameplay loop.

The player initially explores the hotel while it still feels relatively normal.

After the outbreak escalates:

- infected begin appearing
- hotel guests and staff are attacked or transformed
- a police cruiser crashes into the hotel entrance and blocks the easiest escape route
- Jim hears the Deadlock Protocol emergency announcement
- the hotel becomes an interconnected puzzle environment

The hotel introduces:

- exploration
- locked doors
- key items
- puzzles
- limited resources
- creature encounters
- backtracking
- survivor encounters
- environmental storytelling

Jim begins with a baseball bat before eventually gaining access to firearms.

The hotel chapter eventually leads Jim through the courtyard and out toward the center of Ravenwood.

==================================================

MEMORIAL PARK HUB

==================================================

After escaping the hotel, Jim reaches Memorial Park.

Memorial Park becomes the central hub for the Ravenwood portion of the game.

At the center of the park is a monument surrounded by water.

The park connects to several major districts of Ravenwood.

Jim must explore these locations and recover a series of CRESTS.

The crests are tied to Ravenwood's history and to the mechanism hidden beneath Memorial Park.

There are five major crest locations.

==================================================

THE FIVE MAJOR LOCATIONS

==================================================

POLICE STATION

The Police Station represents the collapse of law and order in Ravenwood.

The player explores the station, learns more about the early stages of the outbreak, encounters survivors and infected officers, and uncovers information about the quarantine.

A crest is recovered here.

---

HOSPITAL

The hospital shows the medical side of the disaster.

The player discovers how quickly doctors became overwhelmed and begins finding evidence that the outbreak is stranger than a normal infection.

Medical records and experiments begin pointing toward Vanguard and Project Ashen.

A crest is recovered here.

---

ACADEMY

The Academy explores Ravenwood's history and provides more information about the town itself.

The player encounters abandoned classrooms, institutional areas, survivors, creatures, and clues connecting Ravenwood's past to the current disaster.

A crest is recovered here.

---

FOUNDRY / REFINERY

The industrial district explores Ravenwood's industrial history and its possible connections to Vanguard operations.

This area has a heavier industrial survival-horror atmosphere with machinery, hazardous environments, maintenance areas, and mutated creatures.

The player learns more about activity beneath Ravenwood.

A crest is recovered here.

---

MONASTERY

The Monastery sits farther north near the ridge overlooking Ravenwood.

It provides a darker and more isolated chapter with its own atmosphere, history, puzzles, survivors, and creatures.

Despite its appearance, the story remains grounded in biological and scientific horror rather than supernatural explanations.

A crest is recovered here.

==================================================

CREST PROGRESSION

==================================================

The player can explore the major Ravenwood locations in a semi-open order.

Each major location contains one crest.

The five crests are:

- Police Station Crest
- Hospital Crest
- Academy Crest
- Foundry/Refinery Crest
- Monastery Crest

Returning all five crests to Memorial Park activates the hidden mechanism beneath the central monument.

The water surrounding the monument drains.

A spiral staircase is revealed beneath Memorial Park.

This becomes the entrance to the underground section of the game.

==================================================

VANGUARD / UNDERGROUND FACILITY

==================================================

Beneath Ravenwood is a Vanguard BioSystems facility connected to Project Ashen.

This is where the story shifts from surviving the surface outbreak to discovering the truth behind it.

Jim learns that Ravenwood's disaster was not a random zombie outbreak.

The mutations are connected to Vanguard research involving Black Vein and Project Ashen.

Black Vein is tied to unusual regenerative and mutative properties.

Vanguard attempted to exploit these properties through Project Ashen.

Something went catastrophically wrong.

Containment failed.

The outbreak spread through Ravenwood.

The underground facility reveals:

- the origins of Project Ashen
- Vanguard's involvement
- the true nature of the mutations
- the experiments performed beneath Ravenwood
- why Deadlock Protocol was activated
- how the surface locations connect to the larger conspiracy

The creatures encountered throughout the game ultimately trace back to the same underlying research.

==================================================

ENDGAME

==================================================

The underground facility becomes the final major section of the story.

Jim must survive the remaining Vanguard experiments, uncover the final truth about Ravenwood, and find a way out before the situation becomes impossible to contain.

The story ultimately returns to Jim's original motivation:

Survive Ravenwood.

Escape the quarantine.

Get back to Sarah.

Retired military covers the survival instincts, the calm under pressure, the ability to pick up a baseball bat and keep moving. The civilian job explains why he's out here as an ordinary person rather than someone who would be called in to handle a situation like this.

#### OPTION A — FIELD SYSTEMS ENGINEER / INFRASTRUCTURE CONSULTANT

**What he does:** Travels to remote sites assessing, installing, or troubleshooting industrial systems — power grids, utility infrastructure, communications networks.

- Explains solo travel through rural areas naturally

## PART 3 — DIALOGUE REWRITE PHILOSOPHY

Since you want to rewrite everything to feel less robotic and flat, here is the guiding principle I'll use for every scene going forward:

---

### THE PROBLEM WITH THE CURRENT DIALOGUE

The manuscript dialogue reads like this in many places:

> *SARAH: "You should've stopped hours ago."*
>
> *JIM: "Yeah well, GPS said another hour."*
>
> *SARAH: "Storm bad?"*
>
> *JIM: "Visibility went to shit about twenty miles back."*

Each line is a direct response to the one before it. It's clean and clear but it sounds like two people exchanging information rather than two people who have been married long enough to talk over each other.

---

### WHAT REAL DIALOGUE SOUNDS LIKE

Real conversations between people who know each other well have:

- **Interruptions and overlaps** — they don't wait for full sentences
- **Non-sequiturs** — they respond to what they were thinking, not just what was said
- **Running jokes and shorthand** — references only they understand
- **Unfinished thoughts** — because the other person already knows where it's going
- **Emotion underneath ordinary words** — Sarah isn't just asking if the storm is bad. She's asking because she's worried and won't fully say it.

---

### EXAMPLE — SARAH PHONE CALL REWRITE

**Current version:**

> *SARAH: "You still driving?"*
>
> *JIM: "Unfortunately."*
>
> *SARAH: "Jim, it's almost midnight."*
>
> *JIM: "I noticed."*
>
> *SARAH: "You should've stopped hours ago."*

**Proposed rewrite:**

> *SARAH: "Please tell me you're parked somewhere."*
>
> *JIM: "Technically I'm moving."*
>
> *SARAH: "Jim."*
>
> *JIM: "It's fine. GPS says another hour."*
>
> *SARAH: "Your GPS took you through a cornfield in Ohio."*
>
> *JIM: "That was one time and the road was technically—"*
>
> *SARAH: "It was a cornfield."*
>
> A beat. Rain hammers the windshield.
>
> *JIM: "Visibility's bad. I'll pull over if it gets worse."*
>
> *SARAH: "It already sounds worse."*
>
> *JIM: "Sarah."*
>
> *SARAH: "I know. I know. Just—"*
>
> She doesn't finish it.
>
> *JIM: "I know."*

---

The difference is that Sarah and Jim have **history**. They have shorthand. She doesn't need to say *"I'm worried about you"* — it's in the unfinished sentence. He doesn't need to say *"I'll be fine"* — they both know that's what *"I know"* means.

This is the tone we should hit throughout — every conversation should feel like it belongs to **these specific people** rather than to **a game tutorial.**

## CODEX SECTION 1 — STORY OVERVIEW

### Premise

*Deadlock Protocol* follows **Jim Mercer** — a retired military telecommunications field engineer traveling alone through rural Appalachia during a severe storm.

Flooding and worsening road conditions force Jim off Highway 13 and into the isolated mountain town of **Ravenwood**. He stops at the **Ravenwood Hotel** for what he believes will be a single overnight stay.

The situation deteriorates rapidly.

An outbreak connected to **Vanguard BioSystems** and **Project Ashen** has begun spreading through Ravenwood. People begin mutating into violent creatures. Public order collapses. Authorities initiate **Deadlock Protocol** — effectively quarantining the entire town.

Jim is not a soldier sent to investigate. He is an ordinary man trapped in the wrong place at the wrong time — trying to survive, understand what is happening, and get back to his wife Sarah.

---

### Core Themes

- Isolation
- Survival under pressure
- Corporate conspiracy
- Civil collapse
- Infection and mutation
- Ordinary person in extraordinary circumstances
- Gradual discovery of hidden truth

---

### Tone

- Grounded biological and scientific horror
- The outbreak is **not** supernatural, demonic, fungal, or alien
- Vanguard BioSystems, Project Ashen, and Black Vein are the scientific foundation of Ravenwood's disaster
- Horror emerges from atmosphere, tension, and human consequence — not from manufactured jump scares or clichés

Beside the generator — a maintenance shed. Heavy padlocked doors. Something has warped them badly from inside.

Jim looks at the shed for a moment.

Then he goes to work on the generator.

---

> **SCENE S19 — GENERATOR RESTORATION**

The generator hasn't been started in a while — that much is obvious. Fuel valve partially closed. Pressure dropped. Ignition contacts corroded at the terminals.

Jim works through it methodically. Fuel valve open. Terminals cleaned with what he has available. Pressure checked. Ignition primed.

He's done this kind of thing in worse conditions than a rainstorm in a hotel courtyard. Different equipment, different location, same basic logic — find the problem, address it in the right order, don't rush the steps.

He hits the ignition.

The generator turns over. Coughs. Dies.

He adjusts the choke. Tries again.

The generator roars to life.

The entire courtyard shakes from the startup. Floodlights along the hotel walls blaze on at full power — the courtyard suddenly too bright after hours of emergency red. The gate system begins powering back online.

For a moment — just a moment — the only sound is the generator and the rain.

Then —

**BANG.**

---

> **SCENE S20 — THE CARETAKER**

The maintenance shed doors buckle outward. The chain pulls taut — holds — then snaps.

The doors come open.

He fills the doorway before he steps through it. Maintenance overalls, darkened with water and worse. What the infection has done to him has not finished doing it — the proportions are wrong, one shoulder built up into something that shouldn't fit through a standard doorframe and barely does. His right arm hangs heavier than an arm should hang. The skin is waterlogged and pale in the floodlights. One eye glows faintly — not a color that belongs in an eye.

He steps out into the rain.

Looks at Jim.

A sound comes from somewhere deep in his chest — low and wet and deliberate.

---

*Boss encounter begins.*

---

**PHASE 1 — STALK**

He moves across the flooded courtyard pavement with the patience of something that has decided where it's going and sees no reason to hurry. Wide. Deliberate. Obstacles — a bench, the fountain's edge, a section of hedge — he moves around them or through them depending on which is faster.

Jim keeps distance. The handgun is an option. So is the bat. Neither one feels adequate from where he's standing.

**PHASE 2 — AGGRESSION**

When he closes the distance he commits to it completely. The overhead slam drives into the stone hard enough to crater it. The horizontal swing clears a radius that Jim has to already be outside of before it starts. A shoulder charge that covers ground faster than the rest of his movement suggests is possible.

The recovery windows are real. The attacks have weight — they commit the full mass of him to the motion and then they have to stop. That's when Jim moves.

**PHASE 3 — ENRAGED**

At some threshold the patience breaks. The deliberate stalking becomes something more reckless — charges that don't slow down when they miss, slam combinations without the pause between them, movement that stops caring about obstacles and goes through them instead.

The generator floodlights flicker. The courtyard dims and blazes in uneven intervals. Lightning overhead. The rain driving sideways now.

Jim doesn't stop moving.

---

*The Caretaker goes down.*

---

The courtyard falls quiet except for the generator and the rain.

Jim stands in the middle of the wet stone and the overturned furniture of the fight and breathes.

He looks at what's left of the Caretaker.

He doesn't look long.

---

> **SCENE S21 — NORTH GATE / EXIT INTO RAVENWOOD**

The north gate system is fully active now.

*Interaction prompt:*
***[OPEN GATE]***

The gate mechanism engages — heavy and slow, the groan of something that hasn't moved in a long time being asked to move now. It swings outward into the storm.

Beyond the gate — Ravenwood.

Dark streets. Standing water across the pavement. A traffic light somewhere down the block swinging on its cable in the wind, cycling through its colors for nobody. Police lights flashing in the distance — one source, then two, then the sound of something that might be sirens and might be something else entirely.

The town is not okay.

Jim stands at the gate and looks at it.

**JIM:**
*"...What the hell happened here?"*

The rain doesn't answer.

He steps through the gate.

## WHAT WE KNOW FROM THE OVERVIEW

## THE DECISIONS

---

### DECISION 1 — THE JOURNEY FROM HOTEL TO MEMORIAL PARK

Jim just walked out of the hotel courtyard into a town that is actively falling apart.

**How does he get to Memorial Park?**

> **Option A — Linear corridor**
>
> The streets between the hotel and Memorial Park are a short directed sequence — not fully explorable, just enough to show Jim what Ravenwood has become before he reaches the park. Infected on the streets. Police tape. Emergency vehicles. The scale of the disaster becomes visible for the first time outside the hotel walls.

> **Option B — Open street exploration**
>
> The streets between the hotel and Memorial Park are partially explorable — a small slice of Ravenwood that Jim can move through before the park. Side alleys, storefronts, abandoned cars. Not a full district but more than a corridor.

> **Option C — Direct arrival**
>
> Short cutscene or transition — Jim moves through the streets and arrives at Memorial Park without a playable street sequence. The journey is implied rather than shown. Gets the player to the hub faster.

---

### DECISION 2 — MEMORIAL PARK FIRST IMPRESSION

When Jim arrives at Memorial Park — what does he find?

The overview establishes the monument and the water surrounding it. But what is the **state of the park** when Jim arrives?

> **Option A — Empty and eerie**
>
> The park is deserted. No survivors. No infected. Just the monument, the water, the storm, and the five district entrances around the perimeter. Quiet in a way that feels deeply wrong after the hotel chaos. Jim is completely alone here.

> **Option B — Active chaos**
>
> The park has infected moving through it. Jim has to navigate or fight his way to the monument. The park feels like an extension of the hotel chaos rather than a transition point.

> **Option C — Survivors present**
>
> Jim finds one or more survivors already at the park when he arrives. This introduces new characters earlier and gives Jim someone to interact with before he starts exploring the districts.

> **Option D — Mix of empty and a single survivor**
>
> The park is mostly empty and wrong — but one survivor is present. Someone Jim can get information from. Establishes that he is not the only person trying to survive Ravenwood.

---

### DECISION 3 — THE MONUMENT

The monument at the center of Memorial Park is surrounded by water and hides a spiral staircase beneath it.

**What is the monument?**

This matters for the story because the crests are tied to Ravenwood's history — and the monument likely is too.

> **Option A — War memorial**
>
> A standard civic war memorial — names of the dead from various conflicts. Common in small American towns. Unassuming on the surface. The hidden mechanism beneath it becomes more disturbing in context — someone built this hiding something.

> **Option B — Founding monument**
>
> A monument to Ravenwood's founders — names, dates, a civic inscription. Connects directly to the town's history and the Academy location. The crests as historical artifacts makes more sense in this context.

> **Option C — Abstract civic sculpture**
>
> Something less specific — a large abstract structure, more artistic than commemorative. Less historical weight but more visually striking.

> **Option D — Something stranger**
>
> The monument is unusual for a small mountain town — oversized, architecturally odd, clearly built with more money and intention than the rest of the town's civic infrastructure. This hints early that Ravenwood has always had something unusual about it. Possibly connected to Vanguard's long presence in the area.

---

### DECISION 4 — THE CRESTS

The five crests are recovered from the five major locations and returned to the monument.

**What are the crests physically?**

> **Option A — Stone or metal civic seals**
>
> Official-looking — like the kind of decorative seal you'd find on a government building or a courthouse. Each one bears the symbol of its location. Functional and grounded.

> **Option B — Historical artifacts**
>
> Each crest is genuinely old — something that predates the current buildings, possibly predates Vanguard's presence in Ravenwood entirely. Their existence in these specific locations is part of the mystery.

> **Option C — Vanguard-connected objects**
>
> The crests were placed in these locations by Vanguard as part of the mechanism they built beneath Ravenwood. They look like civic objects but were engineered specifically for the underground access system. This makes Vanguard's reach feel longer and deeper.

> **Option D — Combination of B and C**
>
> The crests are genuinely historical artifacts — old, predating Vanguard — but Vanguard discovered them and built their underground mechanism to use them as keys. The town's history and Vanguard's conspiracy are intertwined.

---

### DECISION 5 — HOW DOES JIM KNOW TO COLLECT THE CRESTS

Jim is a telecom engineer from out of town. He has no reason to know that five crests scattered across Ravenwood will open a mechanism beneath the park monument.

**How does he learn this?**

> **Option A — Survivor tells him**
>
> A survivor at or near Memorial Park has already figured this out — or has partial information — and shares it with Jim. Establishes a key character early.

> **Option B — Documents at the park**
>
> Jim finds something at Memorial Park itself — a notice, a map, emergency documentation — that points him toward the five locations and what to look for.

> **Option C — He doesn't know yet**
>
> Jim arrives at Memorial Park with no specific objective beyond surviving and finding a way out of Ravenwood. The crest mechanic is discovered gradually — he finds the first one incidentally during exploration and only later understands the full picture.

> **Option D — VERN terminal at Memorial Park**
>
> The VERN terminal at Memorial Park contains partial emergency data that references the five locations and the underground access route. Vanguard's own emergency system inadvertently points Jim toward the truth.

---

### DECISION 6 — THE FIVE DISTRICTS — EXPLORATION ORDER

The overview says the five locations can be explored in **semi-open order.**

**How open is semi-open?**

> **Option A — Fully open from the start**
>
> All five district entrances are accessible from Memorial Park immediately. Jim can tackle them in any order. Each location is balanced to be approachable regardless of when the player goes there.

> **Option B — Two or three available first**
>
> When Jim first arrives at Memorial Park, only two or three district entrances are accessible. The others are blocked — flooded roads, collapsed structures, locked gates. As Jim completes locations and recovers crests, more districts open up.

> **Option C — Suggested order with open access**
>
> All five are technically accessible but the environment suggests a natural starting point — one district entrance is more obvious or less dangerous than the others. The player can ignore the suggestion but most won't.

---

### DECISION 7 — SURVIVORS

The overview mentions survivor encounters throughout Ravenwood.

**How do you want survivors to work in this game?**

> **Option A — Fully interactive NPCs**
>
> Survivors can be found, spoken to, and potentially helped. Some may join Jim temporarily. Some may have information. Some may be in situations where Jim has to decide whether to help them or move on. Their fates matter to the story.

> **Option B — Environmental survivors**
>
> Survivors exist in the world — barricaded in buildings, calling from windows, visible but not always reachable. Some can be interacted with briefly. Their primary purpose is environmental storytelling — showing that other people are trying to survive — rather than deep character development.

> **Option C — Key survivors only**
>
> Most survivors are environmental. A small number — perhaps one per major location — are fully developed characters with their own stories, information, and potential fates. These are the survivors that matter to the narrative.

---

### DECISION 8 — SARAH

After the hotel Jim has no contact with Sarah.

**Does Sarah appear again before the ending?**

> **Option A — No**
>
> Sarah is not seen or heard from again until she arrives in Ravenwood at the game's end. Her absence is felt throughout. Jim's motivation to survive and get back to her is internal — carried by the player rather than reinforced by contact.

> **Option B — Brief radio contact**
>
> At some point during the Ravenwood exploration Jim gets a brief broken radio contact with Sarah — not a full conversation, just enough to know she's out there and looking for him. Emotionally powerful precisely because it's incomplete.

> **Option C — One-way communication**
>
> Jim finds evidence that Sarah has been trying to reach him — voicemails on a recovered phone, a message on a VERN terminal, a note left somewhere. He can't respond. She doesn't know if he's alive. He knows she's coming.

## *Deadlock Protocol* — Honest Design Discussion

---

## YOU'RE ABSOLUTELY RIGHT

This is one of the most honest and self-aware things you can say about this kind of game design.

Resident Evil is the perfect reference point.

Nobody in Raccoon City sat down and said —

> *"You know what this police station needs? A giant chess puzzle and a statue that dispenses medallions."*

It's there because it's a game. The player accepts it because the atmosphere is strong enough and the mechanics are satisfying enough that the logical gap doesn't matter. Nobody asks why the Spencer Mansion has a giant rotating room. They just enjoy it.

**Deadlock Protocol can operate the same way.**

---

## THE HONEST ANSWER

The emblems are distributed across five locations and slotted into a statue mechanism because:

- It gives the player a clear long-term objective
- It structures exploration across the five districts
- The payoff — the water draining, the staircase revealed — is satisfying
- The atmosphere and lore surrounding it makes it feel earned

**The in-world justification doesn't need to be airtight.**

It just needs to be present enough that the player doesn't actively question it.

---

## THE MINIMUM JUSTIFICATION NEEDED

Here's the lightest possible in-world logic that makes it feel intentional without over-explaining:

> The founders built the underground facility beneath Memorial Park. The statue and the emblem mechanism were their access control system — crude by modern standards but deliberate. Each founder kept their emblem at the institution they controlled. Over generations the original purpose was forgotten. The emblems became artifacts — kept out of tradition or civic pride without anyone fully understanding why.

That's it. That's all the justification needed.

It gets mentioned once — in a document somewhere — and never belabored. The player accepts it and moves on.

---

## EMBLEM APPEARANCE — CONFIRMED DIRECTION ✅

Given that the emblems were made alongside the statue by the founders — they should feel:

- **Old** — genuinely old, not decorative-old
- **Deliberate** — clearly made to fit something specific
- **Distinct** — each one slightly different because each founder made theirs

**CONFIRMED DESIGN:**

Each emblem is a **cast metal piece** — dark and heavy, the size of a large hand. The shape is a section of the pentagon — one of five. The edges are machined to fit precisely against the neighboring sections.

The face of each emblem bears:

- A **relief portrait** of the founder it represents — their face cast into the metal
- Their **name** along the bottom edge in small capital letters
- A **small symbol** representing their institution — a key for the Police, a serpent for the Hospital, a torch for the Academy, an anvil for the Foundry, a cross or similar for the Monastery

When all five are inserted into the statue plaque — five founder portraits surround the completed pentagon. Five faces looking outward from the center of the town they built.

The mechanism beneath activates not because of any technology — just a weight and pressure system built into the base. Old. Simple. Reliable across generations.

---

## THE IN-GAME DOCUMENT THAT COVERS THIS

Rather than explaining it through dialogue or cutscene — one document somewhere in the game handles the justification cleanly and moves on.

The best place for it is probably the **Academy** — the research and knowledge institution. An old historical record or founding document that mentions the statue, the emblems, and the underground access in passing — as if it were simply a known fact to whoever wrote it.

Something like:

---

> *The Memorial was completed in the autumn of 1887 alongside the founding of the five institutions. Each founder retained custody of their section of the access seal as agreed. The facility beneath the park was secured accordingly. It was decided that no single founder should hold the means of access alone.*
>
> *— Excerpt, Ravenwood Founding Records, Vol. I*

---

Short. Factual. Never calls attention to itself. The player reads it and the mechanism clicks into place without a lecture.

### DECISION 7 — SURVIVORS

**The question:**
Jim is not the only person alive in Ravenwood. How do survivors work in this game?

**The options:**

> **Option A — Fully interactive NPCs**
>
> Survivors can be found, spoken to, and potentially helped throughout the city. Some may have information. Some may be in situations where Jim has to decide whether to help them or move on. Some may join Jim temporarily. Their fates matter to the story and some may appear again later.

> **Option B — Environmental survivors**
>
> Survivors exist in the world — barricaded in buildings, calling from windows, visible but not always directly reachable. Some can be interacted with briefly. Their primary purpose is environmental storytelling — showing that other people are surviving — rather than deep character development. Jim is essentially alone.

> **Option C — Key survivors only**
>
> Most survivors are environmental — seen and heard but not deeply interactive. A small number — perhaps one per major district — are fully developed characters with their own stories, information, and potential fates. These are the survivors that matter to the narrative. The rest are atmosphere.

> **Option D — Combination of B and C**
>
> The world is populated with environmental survivors throughout — people barricaded in, calling out, visible through windows. But within each major district Jim encounters one key survivor who is fully interactive. That person has a story, has information, and their fate is meaningful. The world feels populated without every encounter requiring deep scripting.

---

### DECISION 8 — SARAH

**The question:**
After the hotel Jim loses all contact with Sarah. She doesn't know if he's alive. He can't reach her. Does that change at any point before the ending?

**The options:**

> **Option A — No contact until the ending**
>
> Sarah is not seen or heard from again until she arrives in Ravenwood at the game's end. Her absence is felt throughout. Jim's motivation to survive is internal — carried by the player rather than reinforced by periodic contact. The reunion at the end hits harder because of the complete silence before it.

> **Option B — Brief broken radio contact**
>
> At one specific point during the Ravenwood exploration Jim gets a brief broken radio contact with Sarah. Not a full conversation — just enough to know she's out there and looking for him. One-sided or nearly so. Emotionally powerful precisely because it's incomplete and Jim can't fully respond.

> **Option C — One way communication**
>
> Jim finds evidence that Sarah has been trying to reach him — voicemails on a recovered phone, a message left on a VERN terminal by someone relaying information, a note left at a location she passed through. He can't respond. She doesn't know if he's alive. He knows she's coming. The audience feels the gap between them without a direct conversation.

> **Option D — Periodic one way messages**
>
> Throughout the game Jim occasionally finds evidence of Sarah trying to reach him — not one single moment but a trail. A voicemail early on. A VERN message mid-game. A physical note left somewhere later. Each one shows her getting closer to Ravenwood and more desperate. By the time Jim exits the underground facility she may already be in the city looking for him.

## DECISION 7 — SURVIVORS — LOCKED ✅

### CONFIRMED CANON

**Two tiers of survivors:**

---

### TIER 1 — KEY STORY SURVIVORS

A small number of fully developed survivor characters who are essential or deeply connected to the narrative.

These characters have:

- Full dialogue
- Their own backstory
- Information relevant to the story
- A meaningful fate

These are locked regardless of player actions — they exist, they matter, they have a defined role in the story.

---

### TIER 2 — CONDITIONAL SURVIVORS

A secondary layer of survivors whose **existence, condition, and fate depend on player actions or inactions.**

**THE CONFIRMED EXAMPLE — LOCKED ✅**

**The Police Station Officer:**

- If Jim goes to the **Police Station first** — a surviving officer is alive inside. Barricaded. Frightened. Possibly armed. Jim can interact with him, get information, potentially help him.
- If Jim goes **anywhere else first** and arrives at the Police Station later — the officer has turned. He's infected. The barricade he built is broken from the inside. Jim finds him as a hostile rather than a survivor.

**This is excellent design for several reasons:**

Reason
Detail

Rewards natural play
Players who follow instinct and go to the Police Station first get a live NPC

Punishes delay without punishing the player
The game doesn't lock content — it changes it

Environmental storytelling
A player who finds him turned can still piece together what happened — notes, the broken barricade, the progression of the infection

Replayability
Players who know the system will sequence differently on a second run

---

### EXTENDING THE CONDITIONAL SYSTEM

This same logic can apply elsewhere throughout Ravenwood.

Some rough examples — not locked yet, just illustrating the system:

> A civilian barricaded in a shop near the Hospital — alive if Jim passes through early, gone or turned if he comes through late in the game

> A Vanguard employee hiding in the Academy — alive and terrified on an early visit, dead by suicide or infection on a late visit — with a note explaining what happened

> Someone trapped in a vehicle near the Foundry — alive and calling for help early, silent and still by the time Jim gets there if he delayed

**The world moves without Jim.**

Time passing — even within a single night — has consequences. Not punitive consequences. Just real ones.

---

### THE RULE FOR CONDITIONAL SURVIVORS

To keep this consistent and fair:

1. **The player always gets the information** — whether a survivor is alive or dead, Jim finds what he needs to know. The alive version gives it directly. The dead version leaves it in notes or environmental clues.
2. **The player is never hard-locked** — no survivor death blocks story progression
3. **The game never tells the player a survivor died because of them** — it just shows what happened and lets the player feel it

## Street Blocking Mechanism — Quick Decision

---

The street needs something that:

- **Blocks east and west movement** on first arrival
- **Forces Jim toward the park entrance** naturally
- **Gets removed or bypassed later** so the street opens up on return visits

---

## THE QUESTION IS HOW IT GETS REMOVED

The block itself is easy — debris, a vehicle, a collapsed structure, police barriers. Any of those work visually and feel grounded in the outbreak chaos.

The interesting decision is **what removes it.**

---

> **Option A — Automatic on park completion**
>
> Once Jim secures the park and activates the VERN terminal — the street automatically becomes passable. No extra step needed. The game simply opens the routes once the hub is established. Clean and simple.

---

> **Option B — Something Jim finds in the guardhouse**
>
> Inside the guardhouse Jim finds a key or a code or a release mechanism that controls a security barrier on the street. The parks department or emergency services installed automated street barriers as part of Deadlock Protocol. Jim disengages them manually from the guardhouse. Slightly more grounded — gives the guardhouse one more function.

---

> **Option C — Physical obstacle Jim clears himself**
>
> A specific obstacle blocks the street — a police barrier arm, a gate, a chained bollard — that Jim can physically interact with and remove once he has explored the park enough to find what he needs. No key required. Just a prompt.

> **Option D — The street was always passable — just felt blocked**
>
> The debris and abandoned vehicles make the street look impassable but Jim can actually squeeze through on foot once the player tries. The linearity on first arrival is purely atmospheric — the environment feels closed without being mechanically locked. On return the player knows they can push through.
